title: The Story of the Woman Who Helped Create Virtual Learning
author: Michael B. Horn
summary: Michael Horn interviews Julie Young, founding CEO of Florida Virtual School and later CEO of ASU Prep Digital, about her book Say Yes: How Virtual Became Reality. Young recounts how an elementary educator with no plan was told by a state commissioner to go make up a new model, and how she began by putting the word student in the center of a table and asking what would change. She describes building a culture modeled on a fun, respectful elementary school and on IBM’s autonomy and remote-work practices, being honest with hires about the trade-off of being available eight to eight, and securing a protected line-item budget that kept the school from taking dollars from traditional schools. Her advice to entrepreneurs is to find mentors and models, know your why, plan for failure, build a bench of future hires, and treat vendors as partners. Asked what she would build today, she describes a hybrid, global learning hub with content designed around student interests and early work with businesses. The full interview transcript is included in the email.
points: Starting with the student at the center of every decision changed almost everything about how a school could be designed, from faculty roles to funding.
Young told prospective hires the trade-offs up front (available 8 to 8, seven days a week, in exchange for flexibility), and also made sure their spouses and children understood.
A line-item appropriation meant the virtual school took no money from existing schools, which blunted opposition until the program was institutionalized.
Her five pieces of entrepreneurial advice are mentors and models, know your why, plan for failure, build a bench of potential employees, and make partners rather than vendors.
quotes: Probably the reason that the book is named Say Yes: How Virtual Became Reality is really about the fact that I didn’t have a plan. I was an elementary teacher. I became an administrator in the elementary world. I liked change.

I put the word student in the middle of a table and I said, if we were going to put the student at the center of every decision we made, what would change? And after a lot of silence, a great conversation about the fact that almost everything would change if we put the student at the center of our decisions.
I wanted to create an organization that I wanted to work in.
A great deal of responsibility was given to the employees with a great deal of autonomy. And so with that autonomy came a great deal of responsibility.
You have to love these kids with all your heart as if they were your own, and you have to be available to them when they need you. And that’s the trade-off.
And I remember him kind of going, Julie, this isn’t about kids. This is about money.
we built a bench of employees, potential employees, so that when the time came that we had an opening and we needed to hire somebody, we were not desperate.
I kind of tell this story in the book about you can’t be what you can’t see. And for me, as a young teenager, what have you, I didn’t see women in business.
